caption_hook: Maryland has shark-tooth cliffs, a dinosaur, a mountain folded like a smile and Washington's marble.

layers.name: CALVERT FORMATION
layers.what: A warm Miocene sea once covered southern Maryland, teeming with sharks, whales and shellfish. Its mud and sand now crumble out of the Calvert Cliffs along the Chesapeake Bay.
layers.bonus: Fossil Ecphora, a snail-like shell from these cliffs, is Maryland's state fossil shell.

layers.name: ARUNDEL FORMATION
layers.what: Rivers and swamps once crossed what is now the Washington-Baltimore corridor. Dinosaur bones and fossil wood are preserved in the clay, long dug for iron ore and brick.
layers.bonus: Astrodon, a long-necked dinosaur found here, is Maryland's state dinosaur.

layers.name: PURSLANE SANDSTONE
layers.hook: A mountain folded like a smile
layers.what: River sand and pebbles built up here, then continental collision squeezed the layers into a giant U-shaped fold. A highway cut slices right through it for drivers to see.
layers.bonus: Interstate 68 cuts straight through Sideling Hill, showing the fold from the car window.

layers.name: COCKEYSVILLE MARBLE
layers.what: An ancient sea laid down limestone that was later heated and squeezed into sparkling white marble. Quarried near Baltimore, it built some of the nation's most famous monuments.
layers.bonus: Maryland marble from Texas, Maryland, faces the Washington Monument in D.C.

layers.name: BALTIMORE GNEISS
layers.what: Deep roots of an ancient mountain range, cooked and stretched into banded gneiss. Pushed back up into domes, it pokes out of stream valleys across the Baltimore area.
layers.bonus: Quarrymen called it blue stone, and it built early Baltimore foundations and curbs.
